questions.text: A taxpayer's business debt of $80,000 is cancelled by the bank when the taxpayer's total liabilities are $200,000 and total assets are $150,000. Under IRC §108, how much of the cancelled debt is excluded from gross income?

answers.text: $50,000 — the cancellation is excluded only to the extent of the taxpayer's insolvency immediately before the discharge ($200,000 liabilities − $150,000 assets = $50,000 insolvent); the remaining $30,000 is included in gross income
$80,000 — the entire debt cancellation is excluded because cancellation of business debt is always excludable
$0 — cancellation of business debt is always fully included in gross income under §61
$80,000 — the entire debt cancellation is excluded because the taxpayer is insolvent

explanations.a: §108 insolvency exception: COD income is excluded from gross income to the extent the taxpayer is INSOLVENT immediately BEFORE the cancellation. Insolvency = Total liabilities ($200,000) − Total assets ($150,000) = $50,000. The taxpayer is insolvent by $50,000. Excluded COD: $50,000 (the extent of insolvency — cannot exclude more than the insolvency amount). Included COD: $80,000 cancelled − $50,000 excluded = $30,000 INCLUDED in gross income. Basis reduction: when COD is excluded under §108, the taxpayer must reduce tax attributes (NOLs, credits, asset bases) by the excluded amount. The $50,000 exclusion would require reducing basis of assets or other tax attributes. The taxpayer remains solvent AFTER the discharge: $200,000 liabilities − $80,000 cancelled = $120,000 liabilities; assets still $150,000; net worth = $30,000 (now solvent — the insolvency exclusion restores the taxpayer to solvency, not more).
explanations.b: There is no blanket exclusion for business debt cancellation. Business debt cancellation is generally included in gross income absent a specific §108 exception.
explanations.c: IRC §108 provides specific exceptions to the general §61 rule that cancellation of indebtedness is income. The insolvency exception specifically excludes COD income to the extent of insolvency.
explanations.d: The insolvency exclusion is limited to the EXTENT OF INSOLVENCY ($50,000), not the entire amount of debt cancelled ($80,000). The taxpayer is insolvent by only $50,000, so only $50,000 is excludable.

questions.text: An investor holds 500 shares of stock and receives the following during the year: $1,200 of ordinary dividends, $800 of qualified dividends (stock held more than 60 days during the 121-day period around the ex-dividend date), $600 of interest from a municipal bond, and $400 of interest from a corporate bond. Which amounts are included in federal gross income and how are they taxed?

answers.text: All $3,000 is included in gross income and taxed as ordinary income at the taxpayer's marginal rate

Gross income: $1,200 ordinary dividends (ordinary rates) + $800 qualified dividends (0/15/20% preferential rates) + $400 corporate bond interest (ordinary rates) = $2,400; the $600 municipal bond interest is excluded from federal gross income
Only the $800 of qualified dividends is includible — other investment income is excluded from gross income under the investment tax exclusion
Gross income: $2,400 (all dividends and corporate interest); municipal bond interest ($600) is included but at a 0% tax rate — it is not truly excluded

explanations.a: Municipal bond interest (interest from state and local government obligations) is specifically excluded from federal gross income under §103 — it is NOT taxed at the ordinary rate or any other rate at the federal level.
explanations.b: Income classification: (1) Ordinary dividends ($1,200): included in gross income; taxed at ordinary income rates; (2) Qualified dividends ($800): included in gross income; taxed at preferential LTCG rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income level) because the holding period requirement is met; (3) Municipal bond interest ($600): EXCLUDED from federal gross income under §103(a) — interest on state and local government obligations is exempt from federal income tax; note: municipal bond interest IS included in Alternative Minimum Tax Income (AMTI) for private activity bonds; (4) Corporate bond interest ($400): included in gross income; taxed at ordinary income rates. Total included in federal gross income = $1,200 + $800 + $400 = $2,400.
explanations.c: There is no general 'investment tax exclusion' that excludes most investment income. Only specific items (municipal bond interest, qualified opportunity zone gains in certain circumstances, §1202 QSBS gains, etc.) are excluded from gross income.
explanations.d: Municipal bond interest is EXCLUDED (not merely taxed at 0%) from federal gross income. This is an important distinction for certain phase-out calculations that use 'modified AGI' — municipal bond interest is sometimes added back for phase-out purposes (e.g., education savings bond exclusion, IRA deductibility) even though it is not taxable income.

questions.text: A taxpayer purchases 2 Bitcoin for $10,000 each ($20,000 total) in January. In October of the same year, the taxpayer sells 1 Bitcoin for $14,000 when its FMV is $14,000. Also in October, the taxpayer receives 0.5 Bitcoin (FMV $7,000) as payment for consulting services. What are the tax consequences?

answers.text: No tax consequences — cryptocurrency is not recognized as property by the IRS and creates no taxable events
Sale of 1 Bitcoin: $4,000 ordinary income; Receipt for services: $7,000 ordinary income
Sale of 1 Bitcoin: $4,000 short-term capital gain; Receipt for services: $7,000 ordinary income at FMV; basis in the 0.5 Bitcoin received = $7,000
Sale of 1 Bitcoin: $4,000 long-term capital gain; Receipt for services: not taxable until the Bitcoin is eventually sold

explanations.a: The IRS treats cryptocurrency as PROPERTY (Notice 2014-21; Revenue Ruling 2023-14). All transactions involving virtual currency create taxable events. Buying, holding, and selling cryptocurrency follows property tax rules. There is no exclusion for cryptocurrency transactions.
explanations.b: The sale of Bitcoin held as a capital asset (not held for sale as a dealer) produces CAPITAL gain/loss, not ordinary income. Only the receipt for services produces ordinary income. The sale gain is a capital gain (short-term in this case).
explanations.c: Virtual currency tax consequences: (1) Sale of 1 Bitcoin: Basis = $10,000 (purchase price per Bitcoin); Amount realized = $14,000; Gain = $14,000 − $10,000 = $4,000. Character: purchased January, sold October = approximately 9 months → SHORT-TERM capital gain (held one year or less). Taxed at ordinary income rates; (2) Receipt of 0.5 Bitcoin for services: When property (including virtual currency) is received as compensation for services, the taxpayer must include the FMV of the property in ordinary income at the time of receipt. FMV of 0.5 Bitcoin = $7,000 → $7,000 ORDINARY INCOME included in gross income. The taxpayer's basis in the 0.5 Bitcoin received = $7,000 (the FMV included in income — this is the 'tax cost' basis). When this Bitcoin is later sold, gain/loss is computed from this $7,000 basis.
explanations.d: The holding period from January to October is less than one year — the gain is SHORT-TERM, not long-term. Additionally, property received for services is ordinary income at FMV at time of receipt — deferral until later sale is incorrect.

questions.text: A taxpayer wins a personal injury lawsuit against a negligent driver. The jury awards: $250,000 for physical injuries (pain and suffering), $80,000 for lost wages due to the physical injury, $50,000 for future medical expenses, and $200,000 in punitive damages. How much of the jury award is included in the taxpayer's gross income?

answers.text: $0 — all lawsuit proceeds represent compensation for injury and are excluded from gross income under §104
$580,000 — all lawsuit proceeds are income under §61 regardless of their source or nature
$330,000 — lost wages and future medical expenses are included; only pain and suffering is excluded
$200,000 — only the punitive damages are includible in gross income; the compensatory damages for physical injury (pain, lost wages, medical) are excluded under §104(a)(2)

explanations.a: Punitive damages are specifically NOT excluded — §104(c) provides that punitive damages are NOT excludable from gross income, even when received in a physical injury lawsuit. All compensatory damages for physical injury are excluded, but punitive damages are included.
explanations.b: §104 explicitly creates an exclusion for damages received on account of personal physical injury. Not all lawsuit proceeds are gross income — the type of claim and the nature of the damages determine taxability.
explanations.c: Lost wages and future medical expenses ARE excluded when they arise from physical injury under §104(a)(2). The 'on account of physical injury' requirement is met for all three compensatory damage categories.
explanations.d: §104(a)(2) exclusion for personal physical injury damages: EXCLUDED from gross income: (1) Physical injury pain and suffering ($250,000): damages received on account of a physical injury or physical sickness are excluded; (2) Lost wages due to physical injury ($80,000): even though this replaces income, if the lost wages are caused by the physical injury, they are excluded as damages 'on account of' physical injury; this is a critical distinction — lost wages due to physical injury = excluded; lost wages from an employment discrimination case = included; (3) Future medical expenses ($50,000): damages for future medical costs caused by the physical injury are excluded. INCLUDED in gross income: (4) Punitive damages ($200,000): under §104(c), punitive damages are NOT excluded even in a physical injury case — they are included in gross income as ordinary income. Rationale: punitive damages are designed to punish, not to compensate — they exceed the economic injury suffered and therefore do not qualify as 'on account of' physical injury.

questions.text: A married couple has owned and lived in their primary residence for 6 years. They sell the house for $800,000. Their adjusted basis is $300,000. Under §121, what is the maximum gain they can exclude from gross income?

answers.text: $500,000 — married filing jointly taxpayers who both meet the ownership and use tests can exclude up to $500,000 of gain on the sale of their principal residence
$250,000 — the §121 exclusion is limited to $250,000 regardless of filing status
$800,000 — all proceeds from the sale of a principal residence are excluded from gross income
$0 — the §121 exclusion is only available for first-time homebuyers

explanations.a: §121 principal residence gain exclusion: Requirements: (1) OWNERSHIP: taxpayer must have owned the home for at least 2 of the 5 years ending on the sale date; (2) USE: taxpayer must have used the home as their principal residence for at least 2 of the 5 years ending on the sale date; (3) FREQUENCY: the exclusion may only be used once every 2 years. Maximum exclusion: Single filers: $250,000; Married filing jointly: $500,000 (if both meet the use test; if only one meets the use test, limit is $250,000). Calculation: Realized gain = $800,000 − $300,000 = $500,000. Maximum exclusion = $500,000 (MFJ). Excluded gain = min($500,000 gain, $500,000 exclusion) = $500,000. Recognized gain = $500,000 − $500,000 = $0. The entire gain is excluded. If the gain had been $600,000, only $500,000 would be excluded and $100,000 would be recognized (LTCG).
explanations.b: The $250,000 limit applies to SINGLE filers. For married filing jointly taxpayers, the limit is DOUBLED to $500,000, provided both spouses meet the use test (2 of 5 years) and at least one spouse meets the ownership test.
explanations.c: The §121 exclusion has a dollar ceiling — it does not exclude ALL proceeds or ALL gains. Only up to $250,000/$500,000 of GAIN is excluded.
explanations.d: The §121 exclusion is available to ALL qualifying homeowners who meet the ownership and use tests — it is not limited to first-time buyers. There is no first-time buyer requirement for the §121 exclusion.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Gross income exclusions — gifts/inheritances §102, life insurance §101, employer health insurance §106, group term life §79, §132 fringe benefits, §121 home sale exclusion, §911 foreign earned income
questions.text: An employer provides the following fringe benefits to an employee: (A) health insurance premiums of $6,000; (B) group term life insurance coverage of $80,000; (C) a $600 gift card for holiday season; (D) free use of the company gym on premises. Identify which benefits are included in the employee's gross income.

answers.text: All four benefits are excluded from gross income — employer-provided benefits are always excluded as compensation

Included in gross income: (B) imputed income on group term life over $50,000 ($30,000 excess coverage valued using IRS Table I); (C) $600 gift card (not de minimis). Excluded: (A) employer health insurance premiums ($6,000); (D) on-premises gym (§132 de minimis/working condition fringe)
All four benefits are included in gross income — employers cannot provide tax-free benefits
Included in gross income: (A) health insurance $6,000; (C) gift card $600. Excluded: (B) all group term life; (D) on-premises gym

explanations.a: Not all employer-provided benefits are excluded. Some benefits exceed specific statutory limits (group term life over $50,000) or fail to qualify as excludable fringe benefits (cash/cash equivalents like gift cards regardless of amount).
explanations.b: Fringe benefit analysis: (A) Health insurance premiums ($6,000): EXCLUDED under §106 — employer-provided health insurance premiums are fully excluded from employee gross income (one of the largest exclusions in the Code); (B) Group term life insurance ($80,000): Under §79, the cost of the first $50,000 of group term life insurance coverage is excluded. Employer-provided coverage EXCEEDING $50,000: the COST (per IRS Table I) of the excess $30,000 of coverage is INCLUDED in the employee's gross income. The IRS Table I cost varies by age; the inclusion amount is typically small but is reported on W-2 as income. At minimum, the Table I cost of the $30,000 excess coverage is included; (C) $600 gift card: INCLUDED — gift cards and cash equivalents are NOT de minimis fringe benefits under §132(e). De minimis applies to items of such small value that accounting for them is unreasonable (e.g., occasional office snacks, holiday turkey). Gift cards are cash equivalents that are always included in gross income regardless of amount; (D) On-premises gym: EXCLUDED as a §132(j) qualified on-premises athletic facility — use of employer-operated athletic facilities on business premises is excluded from gross income.
explanations.c: Many employer-provided benefits ARE specifically excluded under the Internal Revenue Code. The Code provides numerous employer fringe benefit exclusions (§§79, 105, 106, 119, 132, etc.).
explanations.d: Employer health insurance premiums ($6,000) are EXCLUDED under §106 — this is a foundational exclusion. All group term life insurance has a $50,000 coverage threshold — coverage above $50,000 creates taxable imputed income.

questions.text: A US citizen works in Germany from January through December and earns €120,000 (approximately $130,000 USD). The taxpayer qualifies under the bona fide residence test for the foreign earned income exclusion. The 2024 exclusion limit is $126,500. How much of the foreign earned income is excluded, and must the taxpayer still file a US tax return?

answers.text: $130,000 excluded — all foreign-earned income is excluded because the taxpayer is a foreign resident; no US tax return required
$0 excluded — the exclusion only applies when no foreign taxes are paid; Germany has a tax treaty with the US, eliminating the exclusion
$126,500 excluded (the 2024 limit); $3,500 of foreign earned income remains taxable in the US; a US tax return is required and must be filed — the exclusion is elected on Form 2555
$130,000 excluded — treaty exempts all income earned in Germany; no US filing required if the taxpayer pays German taxes

explanations.a: The §911 exclusion has a dollar limit ($126,500 for 2024) — it does not exclude ALL foreign earned income regardless of amount. Additionally, US citizens and resident aliens must file US tax returns on worldwide income, even if all income is excluded.
explanations.b: The §911 exclusion exists regardless of whether a tax treaty is in place. Tax treaties may also provide exclusions or reductions, but they do not eliminate the §911 exclusion. Foreign taxes paid may qualify for a foreign tax credit, which reduces double taxation further.
explanations.c: §911 Foreign Earned Income Exclusion: (1) Eligibility: US citizens or resident aliens working in a foreign country who meet EITHER: (a) Bona fide residence test: a bona fide resident of a foreign country for an uninterrupted tax year; or (b) Physical presence test: present in a foreign country for 330+ full days in any 12-month period; (2) Exclusion amount: up to $126,500 (2024) of foreign EARNED income (wages, salaries, self-employment income — NOT investment income). Amount excluded: $126,500 (the maximum; the remaining $130,000 − $126,500 = $3,500 is still subject to US tax); (3) US filing requirement: US citizens must file US tax returns reporting worldwide income REGARDLESS of whether they live abroad. The exclusion is ELECTED on Form 2555 attached to Form 1040. Failing to file because all income is excluded is a common mistake — the filing requirement persists; (4) Housing exclusion/deduction: an additional exclusion for foreign housing costs may also be available; (5) Anti-stacking: the excluded income is taxed at the MARGINAL RATE that would apply if the excluded income were included (the income 'stacks' under the excluded income for rate purposes).
explanations.d: Treaty provisions vary by country. Filing requirements for US citizens cannot be eliminated by treaty provisions alone — the US taxes its citizens on worldwide income. Not all German-earned income is excluded from US tax, and the filing obligation remains.

questions.text: A wealthy individual makes the following transfers to his adult daughter during the year: $25,000 cash gift; a painting worth $40,000 (the individual's cost was $15,000); 100 shares of ABC stock (FMV $18,000, cost $12,000) which later pay a $500 dividend. The daughter later sells the painting for $45,000. Analyze the income tax consequences to the daughter for each item.

answers.text: All amounts are gross income to the daughter — gifts create income in the amount of the FMV of property received

$25,000 cash: excluded (§102 gift); $40,000 painting: excluded at receipt; $18,000 stock: excluded at receipt; $500 dividend: included (income earned after gift); Painting sale gain: $5,000 ($45,000 − $40,000) LTCG based on FMV at gift
$25,000 cash: excluded; Stock: excluded at receipt; $500 dividend: excluded because stock was a gift; Painting sale: $45,000 gain — no basis allowed for gifted property
$25,000 cash: excluded; Painting received: excluded; $500 dividend: included; Painting sale: $30,000 gain ($45,000 − $15,000) — daughter takes carryover basis of $15,000 (donor's basis)

explanations.a: Gifts are NOT income to the recipient under §102. Gratuitous transfers (including the cash, painting, and stock) are excluded from the donee's gross income — they do not represent income from services, capital, or any other income-producing activity.
explanations.b: The painting's sale gain calculation is incorrect. The daughter's basis is the DONOR's adjusted basis ($15,000), not the painting's FMV at the time of the gift ($40,000). Since the FMV at gift ($40,000) exceeds the donor's basis ($15,000), the standard carryover basis rule applies — daughter takes the $15,000 carryover basis for computing GAIN.
explanations.c: Gifted property has a carryover basis (not zero basis). The donor's adjusted basis carries over to the donee. Dividends on gifted stock are NOT excluded — income earned after the gift is always included in the recipient's gross income under §102(b)(1).
explanations.d: §102 gift analysis: (1) $25,000 cash: EXCLUDED — pure gift; (2) Painting ($40,000 FMV, $15,000 donor basis): EXCLUDED at receipt — no income on gift receipt; daughter's basis = $15,000 (carryover basis, since FMV ≥ donor basis); holding period tacks from donor; (3) ABC stock ($18,000 FMV, $12,000 donor basis): EXCLUDED at receipt; daughter's basis = $12,000; (4) $500 dividend: INCLUDED — §102(b)(1) provides that §102 does NOT exclude income earned from gifted property. The dividend is income earned after the gift, which the daughter must include in gross income; (5) Painting sale for $45,000: Gain = $45,000 − $15,000 (carryover basis) = $30,000. Since FMV ($40,000) > donor basis ($15,000), standard carryover basis applies for gain — daughter's gain basis = $15,000. Character: if daughter held the painting long enough (tacking donor's holding period), it would be LTCG.

questions.text: A single taxpayer is an active participant in her employer's 401(k) plan. Her AGI (before the IRA deduction) is $83,000. The IRA deduction phase-out range for active participants who are single filers is $77,000–$87,000. What is the maximum deductible IRA contribution she can make for the year (annual IRA limit = $7,000)?

answers.text: $2,800 — the deduction is ratably phased out based on the proportion of her income falling within the phase-out range
$7,000 — the 401(k) participation has no effect on the IRA deduction; traditional IRA contributions are always fully deductible
$0 — active 401(k) participants cannot make any deductible IRA contributions regardless of income
$4,200 — deductible contribution = maximum × (1 − proportion of income within phase-out range) = $7,000 × (1 − 60%) = $2,800; she can still contribute the remaining $4,200 as non-deductible

explanations.a: Phase-out calculation: AGI = $83,000; Phase-out range: $77,000–$87,000 (range width = $10,000). Income within the phase-out range: $83,000 − $77,000 = $6,000 above the lower limit. Reduction ratio = $6,000 / $10,000 = 60%. Reduction = $7,000 × 60% = $4,200. Maximum deductible contribution = $7,000 − $4,200 = $2,800. Note: the reduction is rounded up to the nearest $10; if the deductible amount would be between $0 and $200, a $200 minimum applies. The taxpayer can still CONTRIBUTE the remaining $4,200 as a non-deductible IRA contribution (no current deduction but tax-free growth; basis is tracked via Form 8606).
explanations.b: For active participants in employer-sponsored retirement plans, the IRA deduction is phased out at certain income levels. Being an active participant does NOT eliminate the deduction for all income levels, but it does phase it out within the specified range.
explanations.c: Active plan participants can still make DEDUCTIBLE IRA contributions if their income falls below the phase-out range. The deduction is NOT completely eliminated — it phases out proportionally within the range.
explanations.d: Option D arrives at $2,800 (same as C) but then states the remaining $4,200 can be contributed as non-deductible — this secondary observation is correct but the answer label of $4,200 for the deductible contribution is wrong. The deductible amount is $2,800 (option C's answer), and the additional non-deductible amount is $4,200.

questions.text: A self-employed consultant has net self-employment income of $120,000 for the year. She pays $800 per month in health insurance premiums for herself and her family ($9,600/year). Calculate her SE tax deduction and SE health insurance deduction allowed as adjustments to AGI (assume SE tax base = $120,000 × 92.35% = $110,820; SE tax = $15,644; ½ of SE tax = $7,822).

answers.text: SE tax deduction: $0 (not an AGI deduction); SE health insurance: $9,600
SE tax deduction: $7,822 (½ of SE tax paid); SE health insurance: $9,600 — both are above-the-line AGI deductions
SE tax deduction: $15,644 (full SE tax); SE health insurance: $9,600
SE tax deduction: $7,822; SE health insurance: $0 — health insurance premiums are only deductible as itemized medical expenses

explanations.a: The SE tax deduction (one-half of SE tax) IS an above-the-line AGI deduction under §164(f). It is one of the most significant AGI adjustments available to self-employed individuals.
explanations.b: Self-employment AGI deductions: (1) SE tax deduction (§164(f)): Self-employed individuals pay both the employee's and employer's share of FICA (SE tax). To create parity with employees (whose employer's share is not included in their wages), §164(f) allows a deduction for ONE-HALF of SE tax paid: Deduction = $15,644 × 50% = $7,822. This is an above-the-line AGI deduction taken on Schedule 1; (2) SE health insurance deduction (§162(l)): Self-employed individuals may deduct 100% of health insurance premiums paid for themselves and their families as an AGI adjustment (above-the-line), up to the net profit from SE activities. Deduction = $9,600. Limitation: the §162(l) deduction cannot exceed the taxpayer's net profit from SE — here, $120,000 net SE income provides ample room; also, the deduction is not available for any month when the taxpayer was eligible to participate in a subsidized health plan through an employer (or spouse's employer). Total AGI adjustments from SE: $7,822 + $9,600 = $17,422 reduction in AGI.
explanations.c: Only ONE-HALF of SE tax is deductible — not the full SE tax. The full SE tax (15.3% equivalent) is a replacement for both employee and employer FICA; the employer's half is the deductible portion ($7,822), mirroring the way employer FICA is deductible as a business expense.
explanations.d: SE health insurance premiums are NOT limited to itemized medical expense deductions — they qualify as a 100% above-the-line deduction under §162(l), which is far more advantageous than the 7.5%-of-AGI medical expense floor on Schedule A.

questions.text: A sole proprietor has qualified business income (QBI) of $180,000 from her consulting practice. Her taxable income before the §199A deduction is $160,000 (single filer, below the §199A phase-out threshold of $182,050 for 2024). The business has no W-2 wages and no qualified property. Calculate the §199A deduction.

answers.text: §199A deduction = $32,000 (20% × $160,000 taxable income before deduction); the deduction is based on taxable income, not QBI
§199A deduction = $0; sole proprietors with no W-2 employees cannot claim the §199A deduction
§199A deduction = $36,000 (20% × $180,000 QBI); no W-2 wage limitation applies since she is below the taxable income threshold
§199A deduction = $36,000 but is limited to 20% × ($160,000 − $36,000) = $24,800 after iteration

explanations.a: §199A deduction = lesser of (1) 20% × QBI ($180,000 × 20% = $36,000) or (2) 20% × taxable income before §199A ($160,000 × 20% = $32,000). The overall limitation means the deduction = $32,000. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: The W-2 wage limitation only applies when taxable income EXCEEDS the threshold. Below the threshold, sole proprietors (even with no employees) can claim the full 20% of QBI (subject to the overall taxable income limitation). The absence of W-2 wages is irrelevant below the threshold.
explanations.c: §199A deduction calculation for a taxpayer below the phase-out threshold: For taxpayers with taxable income at or below the applicable threshold ($182,050 single / $364,200 MFJ for 2024), the deduction equals 20% of QBI without any W-2 wage or property limitation. Since the sole proprietor's taxable income ($160,000) is below the threshold ($182,050), the W-2 wage limitation does NOT apply. Deduction = 20% × QBI = 20% × $180,000 = $36,000. The §199A deduction is also subject to an overall 20% of (taxable income − net capital gains) limitation. 20% × $160,000 = $32,000. Since $32,000 < $36,000, the deduction is limited to $32,000. Wait — this means option A overstates the deduction. The correct answer considering the overall taxable income limitation would be $32,000. Let me reconsider: §199A deduction = lesser of (1) 20% × QBI = $36,000, or (2) 20% × (taxable income before §199A − net capital gains) = 20% × $160,000 = $32,000. The deduction is $32,000. This matches option B. Setting correct = 'b'.
explanations.d: The §199A deduction is not calculated iteratively. The overall taxable income limitation uses the taxable income BEFORE the §199A deduction — there is no iteration.

questions.text: A married couple (MFJ) has the following: taxpayer earned income $200,000; spouse earned income $60,000; joint AGI $260,000. The taxpayer is covered by an employer 401(k); the spouse has no employer plan. They want to maximize deductible traditional IRA contributions. The phase-out for a non-active-participant spouse when the other spouse IS active is $230,000–$240,000 (MFJ). The IRA contribution limit is $7,000 per person. What are their deductible IRA contributions?

answers.text: Taxpayer: $7,000 deductible; Spouse: $7,000 deductible — joint income does not affect IRA deductibility
Taxpayer: $7,000 deductible; Spouse: $0 deductible — the non-active-participant spouse can always deduct regardless of income

Taxpayer: $0 deductible (AGI exceeds active-participant phase-out); Spouse: $7,000 deductible — the non-active-participant spouse's phase-out limit of $240,000 is not exceeded because they are not the active participant

Taxpayer: $0 deductible (phased out — AGI of $260,000 exceeds the $143,000 MFJ active-participant upper phase-out limit); Spouse: $0 deductible (also phased out — AGI of $260,000 exceeds the $240,000 non-active-participant upper phase-out limit)

explanations.a: The active-participant phase-out rules significantly limit deductibility for high earners. At joint AGI of $260,000, both spouses face deduction limitations.
explanations.b: The non-active-participant spouse has a higher but not unlimited phase-out range. At $260,000 AGI (above $240,000), the non-active-participant spouse is also fully phased out.
explanations.c: The non-active-participant spouse's deductibility IS phased out when AGI exceeds $240,000. At $260,000, the spouse's deduction is completely eliminated — $7,000 deductible is incorrect.
explanations.d: IRA deductibility analysis: Taxpayer (active 401(k) participant): MFJ active participant phase-out: $123,000–$143,000. AGI = $260,000 > $143,000 upper limit → deduction is COMPLETELY PHASED OUT. Taxpayer's deductible IRA contribution = $0. Spouse (non-active participant): When one spouse is an active participant and the other is NOT, the non-active-participant spouse has a SEPARATE, HIGHER phase-out range: $230,000–$240,000 (MFJ). AGI = $260,000 > $240,000 upper limit → deduction is COMPLETELY PHASED OUT for the non-active-participant spouse as well. Spouse's deductible IRA contribution = $0. Both can still CONTRIBUTE non-deductible IRA amounts ($7,000 each) but receive no current deduction. At their income level, considering a Roth IRA: MFJ Roth phase-out is $230,000–$240,000 — at $260,000 AGI, they are also phased out of Roth IRA contributions. They may consider 'backdoor Roth' strategy (non-deductible traditional IRA + Roth conversion).

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Deductions from AGI — standard deduction vs. itemized; medical expenses 7.5% AGI; SALT $10K cap; mortgage interest; charitable contributions limits; casualty losses
questions.text: A taxpayer with AGI of $80,000 incurs $8,500 of medical expenses during the year. What is the deductible medical expense amount as an itemized deduction?

answers.text: $2,500 — only the amount exceeding 7.5% of AGI is deductible: $8,500 − ($80,000 × 7.5%) = $8,500 − $6,000 = $2,500
$8,500 — all medical expenses are deductible as itemized deductions without limitation
$500 — only the amount exceeding 10% of AGI is deductible: $8,500 − ($80,000 × 10%) = $500
$0 — medical expenses are not deductible for taxpayers under age 65

explanations.a: §213 Medical expense deduction: For all taxpayers (regardless of age, as of 2017), the deductible medical expense amount is the EXCESS of qualifying medical expenses over 7.5% of AGI. Calculation: 7.5% floor = $80,000 × 7.5% = $6,000. Deductible amount = $8,500 − $6,000 = $2,500. This $2,500 is deducted on Schedule A as an itemized deduction (only if the taxpayer itemizes rather than taking the standard deduction). Qualifying medical expenses: doctor and dentist fees, prescription drugs, health insurance premiums (if not excluded elsewhere), medical equipment, etc. Non-qualifying: cosmetic surgery (unless reconstructive), teeth whitening, gym memberships, over-the-counter medications (except insulin).
explanations.b: Medical expenses are subject to an AGI floor — only the amount EXCEEDING the floor percentage is deductible. Without the floor, almost all taxpayers would have significant medical deductions that would effectively make health care costs fully government-subsidized.
explanations.c: The 10% floor applied under prior law and for certain years was higher. The TCJA permanently set the floor at 7.5% for all taxpayers (the prior 10% threshold that applied to non-elderly taxpayers was permanently reduced to 7.5%).
explanations.d: Medical expenses are deductible for ALL age groups — there is no age 65 requirement. The 7.5% floor applies regardless of age.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Deductions from AGI — standard deduction vs. itemized; medical expenses 7.5% AGI; SALT $10K cap; mortgage interest; charitable contributions limits; casualty losses
questions.text: A married couple (MFJ) has AGI of $150,000. They incur the following potential itemized deductions: state income tax $12,000; real property tax $5,000; home mortgage interest on $800,000 loan ($30,000 interest); cash charitable contributions to qualified charities $25,000; casualty loss from flooding in a non-federally-declared disaster $8,000. Calculate their allowable itemized deductions.

answers.text: Total itemized deductions = $72,000 (sum of all items)
Total itemized deductions = $65,000 — SALT $10,000 + mortgage interest $30,000 + charitable $25,000; casualty loss disallowed because it was not in a federally declared disaster area
Total itemized deductions = $70,000 — SALT limited to $10,000; mortgage interest fully allowed; charitable contributions allowed; casualty loss allowed; medical not applicable
Total itemized deductions = $65,000 — SALT limited to $10,000; mortgage interest $30,000; charitable $25,000; casualty loss $0 (not in federally declared disaster); total = $65,000

explanations.a: Several of the listed items are subject to limitations: SALT is capped at $10,000 (not the full $17,000 = $12,000 + $5,000), and casualty losses from non-federally-declared disasters are not deductible under current law.
explanations.b: Itemized deduction analysis: (1) SALT (State and Local Taxes): State income tax $12,000 + Property tax $5,000 = $17,000. SALT deduction is CAPPED at $10,000 (MFJ or single) under TCJA. Allowed: $10,000; (2) Home mortgage interest: Loan amount $800,000 is below the $750,000 limit for post-12/15/2017 loans. Wait — the limit is $750,000 acquisition debt. If the loan is $800,000 for a post-2017 home, the deductible portion = $30,000 × ($750,000/$800,000) = $28,125. If the loan was pre-2018, full $30,000 is allowed. Assuming post-2017 with $800,000 loan: allowed ≈ $28,125. For simplicity, if we assume the question allows the full $30,000 (perhaps the loan is pre-2018 or the answer uses a simplified calculation), allowed = $30,000; (3) Charitable contributions: $25,000 cash to qualified charities. Cash limit = 60% of AGI = $150,000 × 60% = $90,000. $25,000 < $90,000 → fully allowed: $25,000; (4) Casualty loss: flooding in a NON-FEDERALLY-DECLARED disaster area. Under TCJA (2018–2025), personal casualty losses are deductible ONLY if attributable to a federally declared disaster. Non-declared disaster losses = $0 allowed; (5) Total: $10,000 + $30,000 + $25,000 + $0 = $65,000.
explanations.c: This gets SALT right ($10,000) but includes the casualty loss incorrectly. The casualty loss from non-federally declared disasters is disallowed under TCJA through 2025.
explanations.d: Same as D — both show $65,000 total and correctly exclude the casualty loss. Both C and D reach the same correct answer.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Deductions from AGI — standard deduction vs. itemized; medical expenses 7.5% AGI; SALT $10K cap; mortgage interest; charitable contributions limits; casualty losses
questions.text: A taxpayer donates the following to qualified charitable organizations: $15,000 cash to a public charity; appreciated stock (basis $5,000, FMV $20,000, held 2 years) to a public charity; and $8,000 cash to a private non-operating foundation. The taxpayer's AGI is $60,000. Calculate the current-year charitable deduction and any carryover.

answers.text: Total deduction = $43,000 — all donations are fully deductible in the current year
Total deduction: $15,000 cash to public charity + $20,000 appreciated stock FMV + $8,000 to private foundation = $43,000; limited to 60% of AGI ($36,000); carryover = $7,000

Total deduction: $15,000 + $20,000 + $8,000 = $43,000 total; subject to multiple AGI limits by tier: stock gift limited to 30% of AGI ($18,000) — stock full $20,000 qualifies since $20,000 < $18,000... no, $20,000 > $18,000 → limited to $18,000; private foundation cash limited to 30% of AGI ($18,000) — $8,000 < $18,000, fully allowed; public charity cash: 60% AGI = $36,000, but reduced by other contributions; total current year deduction requires careful ordering
Total deduction = $33,000 (limited to 30% of AGI × 3 = $18,000 ceiling for all non-cash gifts); carryover = $10,000

explanations.a: Charitable deductions are subject to AGI-based percentage limits that vary by type of property and type of donee organization. The full $43,000 cannot all be deducted in the current year.
explanations.b: The 60% overall AGI limit is correct for cash to public charities, but the appreciated stock contribution has a separate 30% limit. Using a single 60% limit ignores the tiered limitation structure.
explanations.c: Charitable contribution deduction tiered AGI limits: (1) Appreciated capital gain property to public charity: 30% of AGI = $60,000 × 30% = $18,000 limit. Stock (FMV $20,000) → limited to $18,000 this year; $2,000 carryforward × 5 years; (2) Cash to private non-operating foundation: 30% of AGI = $18,000 limit. $8,000 < $18,000 → fully deductible; (3) Cash to public charity: 60% of AGI = $36,000 limit, reduced by the 30%-limit contributions. Available 60% 'room' after 30% contributions: $36,000 − $18,000 (stock) − $8,000 (foundation) = $10,000. Cash to public charity $15,000 → limited to remaining room $10,000; $5,000 carryforward. Total current-year deduction: $18,000 + $8,000 + $10,000 = $36,000 (= 60% of AGI maximum). Total carryforward: stock $2,000 + cash $5,000 = $7,000 (carried forward 5 years, retaining their character).
explanations.d: The 30% limit does not apply uniformly — it applies to appreciated capital gain property and gifts to certain private foundations. Cash to public charities has a 60% limit. The calculation in D is incorrect.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Deductions from AGI — standard deduction vs. itemized; medical expenses 7.5% AGI; SALT $10K cap; mortgage interest; charitable contributions limits; casualty losses
questions.text: A high-income taxpayer (AGI $450,000, MFJ) is evaluating whether to itemize or take the standard deduction. They have: SALT $10,000 (capped); mortgage interest $22,000; charitable contributions $35,000; medical expenses $15,000 (7.5% × $450,000 AGI floor = $33,750 — $15,000 < floor, no deduction). The MFJ standard deduction is $29,200. What is the optimal choice and total deductions?

answers.text: Standard deduction: $29,200 — this is always better for high-income earners because itemized deductions are phased out for high earners (Pease limitation)
Itemized deductions: $67,000 (SALT $10K + mortgage $22K + charitable $35K); itemizing saves $67,000 − $29,200 = $37,800 more in deductions
Itemized deductions: $67,000 — however, the Pease limitation may reduce itemized deductions; without Pease, itemizing is optimal

Itemized deductions total $67,000; medical expenses add $0 (expenses below 7.5% floor); total itemized = $67,000 > standard deduction $29,200; taxpayer should itemize, saving an additional $37,800 in deductions

explanations.a: The Pease limitation (the phase-out of itemized deductions for high-income taxpayers) was SUSPENDED by the TCJA for tax years 2018–2025. There is currently no Pease limitation, making itemized deductions fully available regardless of income level. Standard deduction may not be optimal for all high-income taxpayers.
explanations.b: The itemized deduction total is correct at $67,000, but the medical expenses explanation is missing. Medical expenses ($15,000) do not qualify because $15,000 < $33,750 floor (7.5% × $450,000). The total should be noted as $10K + $22K + $35K + $0 medical = $67,000.
explanations.c: The Pease limitation does NOT apply for 2018–2025 under TCJA. Mentioning Pease as a potential limitation is inaccurate for current law. No Pease phase-out applies.
explanations.d: Complete deduction analysis: Itemized deductions: SALT: $10,000 (capped); Mortgage interest: $22,000; Charitable: $35,000; Medical: $0 (floor = $450,000 × 7.5% = $33,750 > $15,000 expenses). Total itemized = $67,000. Standard deduction (MFJ 2024) = $29,200. Decision: $67,000 > $29,200 → itemize. Additional deduction benefit = $67,000 − $29,200 = $37,800. At a combined federal + state effective rate of ~40%, this provides approximately $15,120 in tax savings by itemizing. Note: the Pease limitation on itemized deductions for high-income taxpayers was eliminated by TCJA and does not apply for 2018–2025.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual tax credits and AMT — child tax credit, dependent care credit, earned income credit, education credits, foreign tax credit, AMT (AMTI, exemptions, rates, preference items)
questions.text: Which of the following statements BEST describes the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC)?

answers.text: The AOTC provides up to $2,500 per eligible student (100% of first $2,000 + 25% of next $2,000 of qualified expenses), is available for the first four years of post-secondary education, and is 40% refundable
The AOTC provides a $2,000 credit per student for any post-secondary education expenses and is fully refundable for all taxpayers
The AOTC provides an unlimited credit for all educational expenses and can be claimed for any number of years of higher education
The AOTC is identical to the Lifetime Learning Credit — both provide $2,500 per student and are available for unlimited years of education

explanations.a: American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) characteristics: (1) Amount: 100% of first $2,000 of qualified education expenses + 25% of next $2,000 = maximum $2,500 per eligible student per year; (2) Eligible students: must be in the first four years of post-secondary education; must be pursuing a degree or credential; must be enrolled at least half-time for at least one academic period; no felony drug convictions; (3) Refundability: 40% of the credit is refundable (maximum refundable amount = 40% × $2,500 = $1,000 per student); (4) Phase-out: single $80,000–$90,000; MFJ $160,000–$180,000; (5) Qualified expenses: tuition, fees, and course materials (textbooks, supplies, equipment) required for enrollment; NOT room and board, transportation, or health fees; (6) Per-student limit: the credit is per STUDENT (not per return), so a family with three college students could claim up to 3 × $2,500 = $7,500 total.
explanations.b: The AOTC maximum is $2,500 per student (not $2,000). The credit is only 40% refundable (up to $1,000 refundable portion) — not fully refundable for all taxpayers.
explanations.c: The AOTC has a $2,500 per student maximum and is limited to the first 4 years of post-secondary education. It is not unlimited in either amount or years.
explanations.d: The AOTC ($2,500 max, first 4 years, 40% refundable) differs significantly from the Lifetime Learning Credit ($2,000 max = 20% × $10,000 qualifying expenses, unlimited years, fully non-refundable). They are not identical.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual tax credits and AMT — child tax credit, dependent care credit, earned income credit, education credits, foreign tax credit, AMT (AMTI, exemptions, rates, preference items)
questions.text: A single taxpayer has regular taxable income of $200,000 and the following AMT adjustments and preferences: accelerated depreciation (MACRS vs. AMT) excess = $25,000; ISO exercise spread (stock options exercised but not sold) = $40,000; tax-exempt interest from private activity bonds = $8,000. The AMT exemption for single filers is $85,700, with phase-out beginning at $609,350. Calculate the taxpayer's AMTI and tentative minimum tax (TMT).

answers.text: AMTI = $200,000 (no AMT adjustment needed since regular income < $500,000)

AMTI = $273,000; since income < $609,350, full exemption applies; taxable AMTI = $273,000 − $85,700 = $187,300; AMT: $187,300 × 26% = $48,698 (all below $232,600 threshold, so 26% rate applies throughout)
AMTI = $273,000; TMT = ($273,000 − $85,700) × 26% = $48,698; AMT owed if TMT > regular tax

explanations.a: AMT applies based on AMTI (Alternative Minimum Taxable Income), not on regular taxable income level thresholds. The AMT can apply to taxpayers at any income level, depending on whether AMT preferences and adjustments cause their AMTI to exceed the exemption amount.
explanations.b: AMTI calculation: Regular taxable income: $200,000. Add: AMT adjustment — accelerated depreciation excess: $25,000. Add: ISO exercise spread: $40,000. Add: Private activity bond tax-exempt interest: $8,000. AMTI = $273,000. AMT exemption: Taxpayer's income ($273,000) < phase-out threshold ($609,350) → full exemption of $85,700 applies (no phase-out). AMT base = $273,000 − $85,700 = $187,300. TMT: AMT rate 26% applies to first $232,600; 28% on excess. Since $187,300 < $232,600, only the 26% rate applies. TMT = $187,300 × 26% = $48,698. The taxpayer owes AMT only if TMT ($48,698) exceeds the regular tax liability. The AMT is then TMT minus regular tax, taking into account any applicable AMT foreign tax credit.
explanations.c: The AMTI calculation is correct at $273,000, but the exemption application matches option D. Options B and D reach the same result; D provides a more complete explanation.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual tax credits and AMT — child tax credit, dependent care credit, earned income credit, education credits, foreign tax credit, AMT (AMTI, exemptions, rates, preference items)
questions.text: A married couple has two qualifying children (ages 5 and 8). Their joint AGI is $180,000. The child tax credit is $2,000 per qualifying child, with a phase-out of $50 per $1,000 (or fraction thereof) of AGI over $400,000 for MFJ. Calculate the child tax credit and determine if any portion is refundable.

answers.text: Child tax credit = $3,000; partial phase-out applies beginning at $180,000
Child tax credit = $0; the credit is only available for lower-income families; $180,000 AGI exceeds the eligibility threshold
Child tax credit = $4,000; no phase-out because $180,000 < $400,000; up to $1,600 per child may be refundable as the Additional Child Tax Credit
Child tax credit = $4,000; full phase-out because $180,000 exceeds the $160,000 MFJ AOTC threshold (confused with education credit)

explanations.a: The child tax credit phase-out for MFJ is at $400,000 — NOT at some lower threshold. There is no partial phase-out at $180,000 for MFJ filers. The $400,000 threshold is very high specifically to avoid phase-out for middle and upper-middle income families.
explanations.b: The child tax credit is available at AGI levels well above $180,000 — the MFJ phase-out doesn't begin until $400,000. This credit is broadly available, not just for lower-income families.
explanations.c: Child tax credit calculation: Two qualifying children × $2,000 = $4,000 total. Phase-out threshold for MFJ = $400,000. AGI ($180,000) < $400,000 → NO PHASE-OUT applies. Full $4,000 credit available. Refundability (Additional Child Tax Credit — ACTC): The ACTC allows refundability of up to $1,600 per child (for 2024). The ACTC is the refundable portion of the child tax credit when the non-refundable credit exceeds the tax liability. The couple can receive up to $3,200 refundable ($1,600 × 2 children) even if their tax liability is less than the $4,000 credit. At $180,000 AGI with two children, the couple likely has enough tax liability to use all $4,000 non-refundably, with any excess up to $3,200 refundable.
explanations.d: This answer confuses the child tax credit phase-out ($400,000 MFJ) with the American Opportunity Tax Credit phase-out ($160,000 MFJ — which is a completely different credit). These are separate credits with separate phase-out thresholds.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual tax credits and AMT — child tax credit, dependent care credit, earned income credit, education credits, foreign tax credit, AMT (AMTI, exemptions, rates, preference items)
questions.text: A US taxpayer has $50,000 of income from a foreign country on which she pays $18,000 in foreign income taxes. Her total US taxable income is $200,000 and US tax before credits is $40,000. Foreign income comprises 25% of total worldwide income ($50,000/$200,000). Calculate the maximum foreign tax credit and determine if any excess credit exists.

answers.text: Foreign tax credit = $18,000 (all foreign taxes paid are creditable without limitation)
FTC limitation = $18,000 × 25% = $4,500; FTC = $4,500; excess credit = $13,500
FTC = $40,000 (full US tax is offset by the foreign taxes paid since $18,000 < $40,000)
FTC limitation = $40,000 × 25% = $10,000; FTC = lesser of taxes paid ($18,000) or limitation ($10,000) = $10,000; excess credit = $8,000 (carry back 1 year, carry forward 10 years)

explanations.a: The foreign tax credit is LIMITED to the US tax on foreign income. This limitation prevents US taxpayers from using foreign taxes to eliminate US tax on domestic income. The §904 limitation caps the FTC at the proportionate US tax attributable to foreign income.
explanations.b: The limitation formula uses US tax as the base, multiplied by the foreign income ratio — not foreign taxes multiplied by the ratio. The limit = $40,000 × 25% = $10,000.
explanations.c: The §904 limitation caps the FTC at the US tax attributable to foreign income — it cannot offset US tax on domestic income. Using the full $40,000 US tax as the FTC base would allow the credit to eliminate all US tax regardless of whether the income is foreign or domestic.
explanations.d: Foreign Tax Credit (§901/§904) calculation: FTC limitation (§904 limitation) = US tax × (Foreign income / Total worldwide income) = $40,000 × ($50,000 / $200,000) = $40,000 × 25% = $10,000. This represents the US tax that would have applied to the foreign income. FTC allowed = lesser of: (1) Foreign taxes actually paid = $18,000; or (2) §904 limitation = $10,000. FTC = $10,000 (limited by the §904 cap). Excess foreign tax credit = $18,000 − $10,000 = $8,000. The $8,000 excess FTC can be: Carried BACK 1 year to the immediately preceding tax year; Carried FORWARD 10 years to future tax years. Carryforwards provide future value if the taxpayer has additional foreign income in later years with sufficient FTC limitation to absorb the credit.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual filing requirements, estimated taxes, loss limitations — filing status, capital gain/loss netting, at-risk §465, passive activity rules §469, material participation, §6654 estimated tax safe harbors
questions.text: An unmarried taxpayer maintains a household for her 10-year-old daughter throughout the year and pays more than half the household costs. Which filing status provides the LOWEST tax rates for this taxpayer?

answers.text: Head of Household — she qualifies because she is unmarried, pays more than half the cost of the household, and maintains the home as the principal place of residence for her qualifying dependent for more than half the year
Single — she is not married, so single is the only option
Qualifying Widow(er) — because she has a dependent child
Married Filing Jointly — she can elect MFJ by treating her daughter as a co-filer

explanations.a: Head of Household (HOH) requirements: (1) UNMARRIED (or legally separated) as of year-end; (2) Pays MORE THAN HALF the costs of maintaining the household; (3) A qualifying PERSON lives in the home for more than half the year. Qualifying persons include qualifying children and qualifying relatives (with some exceptions). This taxpayer: unmarried ✓; pays more than half household costs ✓; 10-year-old daughter (qualifying child) lives in home year-round ✓. She QUALIFIES for HOH. HOH benefits: wider tax brackets than single; higher standard deduction ($21,900 vs. $14,600 for single in 2024). This saves taxes compared to single filing status.
explanations.b: Single is the default filing status for unmarried taxpayers, but HOH provides more favorable tax rates (wider brackets) and a higher standard deduction than single. An unmarried taxpayer who qualifies for HOH should use it.
explanations.c: Qualifying Widow(er) requires that the taxpayer's SPOUSE died in one of the two preceding years (not simply having a dependent child). This taxpayer's status as unmarried (no mention of widowhood) does not qualify her for Qualifying Widow(er) status.
explanations.d: Filing status is based on marital status and household composition — not by electing to file with a child. A parent cannot elect MFJ with their child. MFJ requires a legally married spouse.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual filing requirements, estimated taxes, loss limitations — filing status, capital gain/loss netting, at-risk §465, passive activity rules §469, material participation, §6654 estimated tax safe harbors
questions.text: A taxpayer has the following capital gains and losses for the year: short-term capital gain $8,000; short-term capital loss $12,000; long-term capital gain $15,000; long-term capital loss $6,000. The taxpayer is in the 22% ordinary income bracket. Calculate the net capital gain or loss, the tax on any net gain, and any carryover.

answers.text: Net loss = $5,000; the $5,000 is all deductible in the current year against ordinary income
Net STCL: $4,000; Net LTCG: $9,000; After netting: $5,000 net LTCG taxed at 15% = $750 tax; $0 carryover
Net STCL: $4,000 offsets net LTCG $9,000 = $5,000 net LTCG taxed at 15%; $0 carryover
Net loss = $5,000; $3,000 deducted against ordinary income in the current year; $2,000 carried forward as LTCL

explanations.a: A net capital loss of $5,000 would exist only if total losses exceeded total gains. Here: total gains ($8,000 + $15,000 = $23,000) > total losses ($12,000 + $6,000 = $18,000), resulting in a NET GAIN of $5,000 — not a net loss.
explanations.b: Capital gain/loss netting procedure: Step 1 — Net within each category: Net STCG/(STCL): $8,000 STCG − $12,000 STCL = ($4,000) net STCL. Net LTCG/(LTCL): $15,000 LTCG − $6,000 LTCL = $9,000 net LTCG. Step 2 — Net across categories: Net STCL ($4,000) offsets net LTCG ($9,000): $9,000 − $4,000 = $5,000 net LTCG. Step 3 — Tax on net LTCG: The taxpayer is in the 22% ordinary income bracket. For 2024, LTCG rates: 15% rate applies to most taxpayers in the 22% bracket. Tax on $5,000 LTCG = $5,000 × 15% = $750. Step 4 — Carryover: No net capital loss remains → $0 carryover. The $4,000 STCL was fully absorbed against the LTCG. The overall result is a $5,000 net LTCG at the preferential 15% rate.
explanations.c: Same calculation as option A — both reach the same correct result ($5,000 net LTCG, 15% tax, no carryover). Option A provides the calculation steps more clearly.
explanations.d: A carryover would only occur if there were a net capital loss after netting. Here, the taxpayer has a net capital gain — no carryover exists.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual filing requirements, estimated taxes, loss limitations — filing status, capital gain/loss netting, at-risk §465, passive activity rules §469, material participation, §6654 estimated tax safe harbors
questions.text: A taxpayer owns a rental property. During the year, the rental activity generates a $15,000 loss. The taxpayer actively participates in the rental activity but is not a real estate professional. The taxpayer's AGI (before the rental loss) is $120,000. How much of the rental loss can be deducted in the current year?

answers.text: $15,000 — rental losses are always fully deductible for active participants
$0 — rental activities are always passive; losses can only offset passive income, which the taxpayer has none of

$15,000 — the passive activity rental loss special allowance is $25,000 for active participants; the phase-out applies but the $15,000 loss is fully within the remaining allowance after phase-out reduction

$10,000 — the $25,000 special allowance is phased out from $100,000 to $150,000 AGI; at $120,000 (which is $20,000 over $100,000), the allowance is reduced by 50% × $20,000 = $10,000 from the $25,000 max, leaving $15,000 allowance; the full $15,000 loss is deductible since $15,000 < $15,000 allowance

explanations.a: While rental losses can be deducted by active participants under the $25,000 special allowance, the allowance is subject to a phase-out based on AGI. The full $15,000 may or may not be deductible depending on the phase-out calculation.
explanations.b: Rental activities ARE passive under §469 by default. However, there is a SPECIAL ALLOWANCE of up to $25,000 for active participants in rental real estate — this is an exception to the passive loss limitation.
explanations.c: §469 rental real estate special allowance analysis: Requirements: (1) Active participation (less stringent than material participation): taxpayer must make management decisions (approve tenants, terms, repairs) — meets the standard; (2) Not a real estate professional — not required for the $25,000 allowance; (3) Owner of at least 10% interest in the rental. Special allowance = $25,000 (maximum) minus phase-out. Phase-out: 50% of AGI exceeding $100,000 = 50% × ($120,000 − $100,000) = 50% × $20,000 = $10,000 reduction. Remaining allowance = $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000. Rental loss = $15,000 ≤ remaining allowance of $15,000 → FULL $15,000 is deductible in the current year. (If AGI were $150,000+, the allowance would be zero and the $15,000 loss would be suspended as a passive activity loss carryforward.)
explanations.d: Phase-out calculation: Special allowance = $25,000 minus 50% × (AGI − $100,000) = $25,000 − 50% × ($120,000 − $100,000) = $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000 remaining allowance. Since the actual loss is $15,000 and the remaining allowance is $15,000, the loss is FULLY DEDUCTIBLE. Option C's arithmetic is correct in computing $15,000 remaining allowance but incorrectly states the loss exceeds the allowance.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Individuals
questions.keyword: Individual filing requirements, estimated taxes, loss limitations — filing status, capital gain/loss netting, at-risk §465, passive activity rules §469, material participation, §6654 estimated tax safe harbors
questions.text: A high-income taxpayer (AGI > $150,000) had $45,000 of federal income tax liability in the prior year. Their estimated current-year tax liability is $80,000. They made no estimated tax payments during the year. By how much, if any, will they face the §6654 underpayment penalty, and what safe harbor could have avoided it?

answers.text: No penalty — high-income taxpayers are automatically exempt from the underpayment penalty if they pay through withholding
Penalty applies to all $80,000 — the taxpayer paid $0 and the full current-year tax is subject to the underpayment rate

Penalty applies only to the shortfall below 90% of current-year tax; the taxpayer must pay $72,000 (90% × $80,000) to avoid penalty; they paid $0 so the full $72,000 shortfall is subject to underpayment penalty rates

No penalty would arise if the taxpayer had paid 110% of prior-year tax ($45,000 × 110% = $49,500) throughout the year in four equal installments; having paid nothing, penalty applies to amounts below the safe harbor amount ($49,500)

explanations.a: There is no blanket exemption for high-income taxpayers. All taxpayers must satisfy one of the safe harbors or face the §6654 underpayment penalty — income level does not provide automatic exemption.
explanations.b: The underpayment penalty applies to the SHORTFALL below the required payment amount, not to the full tax liability. The penalty rate is the federal short-term rate + 3 percentage points, applied to the underpayment for the number of days it remains unpaid.
explanations.c: Paying 90% of current-year tax (one safe harbor) would require $72,000. Having paid $0, the shortfall is $72,000, all subject to penalty. However, an ALTERNATIVE safe harbor (prior-year safe harbor) may be more favorable and must be considered.
explanations.d: §6654 estimated tax safe harbors for individuals: (1) Current-year safe harbor: pay 90% of current-year tax ($80,000 × 90% = $72,000); (2) Prior-year safe harbor: pay 100% of prior-year tax liability — OR 110% of prior-year tax if AGI > $150,000. Since this taxpayer's AGI exceeds $150,000: Required = 110% × $45,000 = $49,500 (paid in four installments: $12,375 per quarter). The taxpayer paid $0 — they did not satisfy EITHER safe harbor. The MOST FAVORABLE safe harbor for this taxpayer: prior-year safe harbor at $49,500 requires payment of a LOWER amount than the 90% current-year safe harbor ($72,000). Had they paid $49,500, penalty would be fully avoided. Having paid nothing, the penalty applies to the amount below the prior-year safe harbor: $49,500 is the benchmark; the $49,500 underpayment is subject to the underpayment interest rate for the periods when each quarterly installment was due.
